claims.claim: And names no lead enforcement agency beyond the President and the Treasury.
claims.sourceSpan: the Securities and Exchange Commission shall prohibit the securities of an issuer described in subsection (b) from being traded on a national securities exchange
claims.note: FLAG: the bill DOES name other agencies with operative roles — the SEC (Sec 106 delisting) and the U.S. Trade Representative (Sec 113(b),(e) 'the United States Trade Representative shall modify or adjust any rate of duty'), plus State/Commerce/Energy in consultative roles. The absence claim overreaches. Minor (President/Treasury are the principal sanctions enforcers via IEEPA at Sec 116, and it sits in a gaps/synthesis field), but factually contradicted. VERIFIER RULING (sonnet): CONFIRMED CONTRADICTED and rules MATERIAL -- Sec 106(a) 'the Securities and Exchange Commission shall prohibit the securities of an issuer...from being traded' and Sec 113(b)/(e) 'the United States Trade Representative shall modify or adjust any rate of duty' / '...shall...determine...and impose duties' assign independent, mandatory ('shall') operative enforcement duties to SEC and USTR, not merely consultative roles. Sec 116(a)'s IEEPA implementing authority is expressly limited to 'sections 102 through 111' and Sec 116(b)'s penalty structure to the same range -- EXCLUDING Sec 106, 112, and 113 -- so SEC/USTR enforcement is structurally separate from, not subordinate to, President/Treasury IEEPA authority. This is also the ONLY place in the whole analysis addressing 'who enforces this' -- Sec 106 (SEC) is never positively surfaced anywhere else either (see the Sec 106 coverage-omission row), so the reader gets zero correct information plus one false claim on this point. RULED MATERIAL: false factual assertion in reader-facing content about the bill's enforcement architecture. FIXED (2026-08-12): removed the false enforcement-agency clause from gaps[1]; SEC (Sec 106) and USTR (Sec 113) are named enforcers.

claims.note: FLAG: source targets the 5 largest importers of Russian oil/gas (and top-5 evasion facilitators), not 'allied countries.' The 'allied' descriptor is unsourced and arguably inaccurate (largest Russian-oil importers are typically not U.S. allies). Framing field, minor. VERIFIER RULING (sonnet): CONFIRMED UNSUPPORTED and rules MINOR, not material -- Sec 113(c) defines targets purely by behavior/volume (new purchases of Russian crude/gas + among the 5 largest importers by volume, or top-5 evasion facilitators); no 'allied' criterion appears anywhere in Sec 113, and the largest global importers of Russian oil/gas are not predominantly U.S. allies, so the label is an unsupported and potentially misleading gloss. Ruled MINOR because: (1) it sits only in the softer likelihoodReason political-prognosis field; (2) the correct behavioral criterion ('countries that buy Russian oil or gas') survives in the SAME sentence; (3) the accurate 5-largest-importers/evasion-facilitator criteria are independently and correctly stated in 4+ other rows (top_lines[1].subs[1], sections[0].items[2].detail x2, gaps[0]) a reader can rely on. Recommend cleanup per neutral-presentation practice, but does not meet the material bar. FIXED (2026-08-12): removed the allied qualifier from likelihoodReason.
